blocks.prompt: The Octopus With Three Hearts
blocks.text: An octopus has eight arms. It also has three hearts. Two of the hearts push blood to its gills. The third heart pushes the blood all around its body. Its blood is not red like yours. Its blood is blue. An octopus has no bones. The only hard part is its beak, and the beak is small. So if the beak fits through a hole, the rest of the octopus can squeeze through too. It can slip through a gap the size of a coin. When an octopus is scared, it squirts a cloud of black ink. Then it swims away while the water is dark.

blocks.prompt: The Animal With Three Hearts and Blue Blood
blocks.text: Your blood is red because it carries oxygen using iron. An octopus does the job differently. Its blood carries oxygen using copper, and copper turns the blood blue. Cold sea water does not give up its oxygen easily, and copper blood is good at pulling it out. An octopus also has three hearts. Two of them are small. They sit beside the gills and push blood through them to pick up oxygen. The third heart is bigger. It sends that blood on to the rest of the body. Here is the odd part. When an octopus swims, the big heart stops beating. Swimming wears the animal out quickly. That is why an octopus would usually rather walk along the seafloor on its arms than swim above it. An octopus has no bones anywhere. The only hard piece is a beak, tucked underneath where all eight arms meet, shaped a lot like a parrot's. If the beak fits through a gap, the rest of the octopus can pour through after it.

4.title: The Octopus With Three Hearts
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: About 500 million neurons
Two thirds of them sit in the arms

Three hearts, blue blood, no bones

blocks.prompt: The Arms That Think for Themselves
blocks.text: An octopus is built nothing like you. You keep almost all of your neurons, the cells that carry thought, locked inside your skull. An octopus keeps about two thirds of its neurons out in its eight arms. Each arm has its own cord of nerves and can taste, touch, reach, and grip without waiting for orders from the brain. If an octopus pushes an arm into a crack in the reef, the arm hunts around on its own. The brain does not need to watch. Those arms are covered in suckers, and the suckers are not only for holding on. Every sucker is lined with sensors that taste whatever it touches. An octopus feeling its way over a rock is licking it with hundreds of small tongues at once. It can tell a crab from a stone in total darkness. The skin does something just as strange. Under the surface sit millions of tiny bags of color called chromatophores. Muscles pull each bag open or let it snap shut, and the skin repaints itself in less than a second. Other cells scatter light to add shine, and the skin itself lifts into bumps and spikes to copy the rough texture of coral. An octopus can vanish against a rock while you are looking straight at it. The strangest part is this. Scientists are fairly sure that almost every octopus is colorblind. It cannot see color the way you can, and yet it matches the colors around it almost perfectly. Nobody has fully explained how. One idea is that an octopus reads color with its skin.

5.title: The Octopus With Three Hearts
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Roughly 500 million neurons, only a third in the brain
Our lineages split over 500 million years ago
The coconut octopus carries shells as portable armor

A gland behind the eyes ends her life after brooding
Three hearts, blue blood, no bones

blocks.prompt: Eight Arms, Three Hearts, Two Years
blocks.text: An octopus and a human last shared an ancestor more than 500 million years ago. That ancestor was probably a small flat worm with nothing worth calling a brain. Everything clever that octopuses do, they invented on their own branch of the tree of life, with no help from ours. This is the closest thing to meeting an alien mind that Earth has to offer. The hardware is unfamiliar. An octopus carries roughly 500 million neurons, about as many as a dog, but only a third of them sit in its brain. The rest are spread through the eight arms, which means each arm can taste, feel, and decide for itself. The brain seems to give a general instruction, something like find food in that crack, and the arm works out the rest alone. Biologists still argue about where the octopus ends and the arm begins. The software is unfamiliar too. Octopuses open screw-top jars from the inside. They learn mazes and remember the answer weeks later. In one laboratory, octopuses learned to tell their keepers apart and squirted cold water at the keeper they disliked. Off the coast of Indonesia, a species called the coconut octopus collects empty coconut shells, cleans them out, carries them stacked under its body across open sand, and assembles them into a shelter when it needs one. Carrying a shell is slow and clumsy, and it protects the animal from nothing while it is being carried. The octopus is paying a cost now for a benefit later, and that is one of the standard tests for using a tool. And then there is the ending. Almost every octopus lives one or two years. A female lays her eggs, fastens them to the roof of a den, and guards them without ever leaving to hunt. She fans clean water over them for weeks or months. By the time they hatch, she is starved and worn out, and she dies. This is not bad luck. A gland behind her eyes drives it. In the laboratory, scientists have removed that gland, and the females went back to eating and lived far longer than they ever would in the sea. So the cleverest animal without a backbone gets almost no time to be clever, and it never meets its own young. Nothing it learns is passed down. Every octopus starts from nothing, works the ocean out alone, and takes what it knows with it.

6.title: The Octopus With Three Hearts
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Class Cephalopoda, order Octopoda
About 500 million neurons, two thirds in the arms
Chromatophores, reflecting cells, and skin papillae
One visual pigment: almost certainly colorblind
Semelparous: one brood, then death
Wodinsky, 1977: removing the optic gland extended life

blocks.prompt: The Mind That Earth Invented Twice
blocks.text: Somewhere around 550 million years ago, a small flat animal in a shallow sea gave rise to two lines of descendants. One line eventually produced fish, frogs, dogs, and you. The other produced snails, clams, and the octopus. At the moment of that split, neither branch had anything worth calling a brain. Complex intelligence had not been invented yet. It would be invented twice, independently, on two branches that never met again. This is why biologists reach for the word alien when they describe an octopus. It is the only intelligence on Earth that owes nothing to ours. Start with the body, because the body explains a great deal. An octopus has no skeleton. Its only hard part is a beak, and a beak is a small thing, so any gap the beak clears the animal can pour itself through. Freedom like that comes at a price. There is nothing to brace against, no fixed joints, no fixed length, and an almost infinite number of ways to bend. A human arm has about seven degrees of freedom, and your brain finds that hard enough to manage. An octopus arm has effectively unlimited ones, and there are eight of them. Evolution's answer was to stop trying to run everything from the top. Of the roughly 500 million neurons in an octopus, around two thirds live in the arms rather than the brain. Each arm carries its own nerve cord, tastes with every sucker, and can run a search, a grab, and a rejection without consulting the brain at all. A severed arm will still reach for food. The brain appears to hand down goals rather than commands, and the arms fill in the details. Whether that means an octopus has one mind or nine is not a settled question, and it may not even be a good question. The skin is a second surprise. Beneath it lie millions of chromatophores, elastic sacs of pigment ringed by muscles that stretch them open in under a second, along with reflecting cells that scatter light and muscles that raise the skin into ridges and spikes. An octopus can match the color, the brightness, and the texture of a rock while you watch, then walk off it and do the same to sand. Yet the eye of almost every octopus contains only a single kind of light-sensing pigment, which should leave the animal colorblind. A colorblind animal is running the best color display in the ocean. One leading explanation is that its strange dumbbell-shaped pupil smears colors apart at slightly different focus depths, so the animal reads color by focusing rather than by comparing. Another is that the skin itself is light-sensitive and reads what the eyes cannot. Neither has been proven. For all of that, the octopus is granted almost no time. Most species live one or two years. Reproduction ends the animal. A female fastens her eggs to the roof of a den, then guards, cleans, and fans them for weeks or months, does not hunt, and dies at about the time they hatch. This is not simple exhaustion. It is programmed. A gland behind the eyes releases the signal, and when Jerome Wodinsky removed that gland from brooding females in 1977, they left their eggs, began eating again, and lived on. So the most intelligent animal without a backbone is given two years, dies alone in a den, and teaches its young nothing, because it never meets them. Whatever an octopus works out about the world, it works out from scratch, and the knowledge dies with it. Culture is impossible. Every generation begins again at zero. The wonder is not that octopuses are clever. It is how clever they manage to become in the time they are allowed.
